claims.text: Reducing bilayer thickness increases interface density in HEA multilayer coatings.
Higher interface density impedes dislocation glide.
Higher interface density impedes dislocation climb.
Impeding dislocation glide and climb reduces creep rates and increases resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
The proposed interface-controlled behavior applies at intermediate temperatures of 300–600 °C.
The relevant initial materials include AlCoCrFeNi- or CoCrFeNi-based multilayer coatings with bilayer thicknesses of approximately 2–20 nm.
Bilayer thickness can be varied while total coating thickness and composition are held constant to isolate interface-density effects.
Elevated-temperature nanoindentation creep can measure time-dependent deformation in HEAs.
Dense nanoscale interfaces between adjacent HEA layers act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Creep deformation in HEAs can be governed by dislocation-mediated processes, including stress-assisted dislocation climb.
Dislocations encountering multilayer interfaces are hindered from further motion or cross-interface glide.
Interface confinement slows dislocation-mediated creep.
Coatings with 2–5 nm bilayers should have lower indentation creep rates than coatings with thicker bilayers or monolithic HEA coatings.
The creep-rate reduction in 2–5 nm bilayer coatings could be several-fold.
High-interface-density coatings should exhibit dislocation pile-ups at or near interfaces.
A monolithic HEA coating of equivalent composition should exhibit higher time-dependent creep deformation than the multilayer coatings.
The interface-density effect may weaken above 600 °C because interface instability or diffusion-mediated mechanisms may become dominant.
The interface-density effect may weaken below 2 nm or above 20 nm bilayer thickness.
Long-term nanoscale-interface stability is uncertain at the upper temperature range and over extended service times.
Interfacial chemical complexity may alter dislocation-interface interactions.
